hints: Look at where cell A sits in Fig. 6.1 - it is the ring of cells just before the xylem with black dots blocking the wall route. What tissue forms that barrier layer?
Follow the solid arrows of pathway B - do they go through the living cytoplasm or stay in the non-living cell walls and intercellular spaces?
walkthrough:
Spot the barrier layer**
Cell A is in the cylinder of cells surrounding the vascular tissue, just outside the xylem. The black dots are the Casparian strip of waterproof suberin. That layer is the endodermis, so cell A is an endodermal cell.

Read the route of pathway B**
The solid arrows stay outside the cell surface membranes, moving through cell walls and intercellular spaces all the way to the endodermis. Movement only through walls and spaces without crossing membranes is the apoplast pathway.
Final answer: cell A: endodermal cell / endodermis; pathway B: apoplast / apoplastic pathway.

hints: Start at the top of the plant - what happens to water on the wet walls of mesophyll cells when stomata are open?
Think about what loss of water from the leaf does to water potential in the leaf compared with the root and soil.
Recall how a continuous column of water in the xylem can be pulled upward without breaking.
Consider which properties of water molecules hold the column together and stick it to the xylem wall.
Link that pull in the stem xylem back to water in the root cortex and how it must move toward the xylem, including at the endodermis.
walkthrough:
Loss from the leaves sets everything going**
Water evaporates from the moist surfaces of mesophyll cells into air spaces and then diffuses out through open stomata as water vapour. That loss lowers the water potential of leaf cells.

A gradient pulls water up**
Because leaf water potential is now much lower than in the stem, root and soil, a water potential gradient is set up from roots to leaves. Water tends to move down this gradient toward the leaves.

Tension in the xylem**
Loss of water puts the water in the xylem vessels under tension. We call this the transpiration pull. It is transmitted all the way down the stem to the root xylem because water forms a continuous column.

Why the column does not snap**
Water molecules stick to each other by cohesion due to hydrogen bonding, and stick to the cellulose and lignin in the xylem wall by adhesion. So when the top is pulled, the whole column is pulled up as one.

Effect across the root**
Pulling water into the root xylem lowers water potential there, so water moves from the higher water potential in root hairs and cortex across to the xylem. At the endodermis the apoplast is blocked by the Casparian strip, so water there moves by osmosis into cells and on to the xylem.

Final answer: Water evaporates from mesophyll cell walls and diffuses out as vapour via stomata; this lowers leaf water potential creating a water potential gradient from roots to leaves. This creates transpiration pull / tension in xylem. Cohesion by hydrogen bonding between water molecules and adhesion to xylem walls maintains continuous water columns, so water is drawn across the root from root hairs to xylem, moving by osmosis across the endodermis.

hints: Trace the dashed arrows of pathway C in Fig. 6.1 - do they stay in walls or pass through cell contents and from cell to cell?
Think about what slows water down when it has to cross membranes and flow through cytoplasm and vacuoles compared with free flow in walls.
walkthrough:
Identify the two routes**
Pathway B is the apoplast through cell walls and spaces with little resistance. Pathway C is the symplast where the dashed arrows go from cytoplasm to cytoplasm through plasmodesmata.

Why membranes slow flow**
In pathway C water must cross cell surface membranes and move by osmosis through cytoplasm and sometimes vacuoles. Crossing membranes and flowing through living contents gives much greater resistance, so movement is slower than in pathway B.

Final answer: Pathway C (symplast) is slower because water passes through cytoplasm / plasmodesmata / vacuoles and across cell surface membranes by osmosis, giving greater resistance than free movement in walls in pathway B.

hints: Compare the direction of ion movement relative to the concentration gradient in each process - which one can push ions uphill?
Think about energy and proteins - which process needs ATP and which uses only channel or carrier proteins without metabolic energy?
walkthrough:
Direction and energy**
In facilitated diffusion ions simply move down their concentration gradient through proteins, so it is passive and needs no ATP. In active transport ions are pumped against their concentration gradient, which needs energy from ATP and respiration.

Protein involvement**
Both use membrane proteins, but facilitated diffusion relies on channel proteins and carrier proteins to let ions through down the gradient. Active transport must use specific carrier proteins that change shape using ATP to push ions uphill.

Final answer: Facilitated diffusion moves ions down a concentration gradient and is passive requiring no ATP / metabolic energy, whereas active transport moves ions against a concentration gradient using ATP. Facilitated diffusion uses channel and carrier proteins only.
